prompt.context_jp: 張りつめた空気の中、舞の目___ある一瞬の動きをとらえた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 舞の目___ある一瞬の動きをとらえた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that marks Mai's eyes catching a new, decisive movement in the scene.

feedback.correct_en: This is a narrative beat where the action itself is the news — Mai's eyes catching the movement is the moment the scene turns. が foregrounds that fresh event.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn 舞の目 into a stated topic, as if we had been discussing her eyes; the sentence is instead reporting a sudden observation. を can't mark the subject here.

contrast_examples.jp: 舞の目がある一瞬の動きをとらえた。
contrast_examples.en: Mai's eyes caught a fleeting movement. (reporting the event)

contrast_examples.jp: 舞の目はいつも鋭い。
contrast_examples.en: Mai's eyes are always sharp. (describing an established topic)

prompt.context_jp: 客一人ひとりに気を使いながらも、処理の速さ___誰にも引けを取らなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 処理の速さ___誰にも引けを取らなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits here, where the narrator is characterizing Kyoko's processing speed?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence sets 処理の速さ up as the topic being evaluated — 'as for her speed, no one could match it.' は is the natural topic marker for this kind of general assessment.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it sound like fresh news that her speed was unmatched, but the surrounding text is describing her overall capability. に is ungrammatical as a subject marker.

contrast_examples.jp: 処理の速さは誰にも引けを取らなかった。
contrast_examples.en: As for her speed, no one could match it.

contrast_examples.jp: 処理の速さが問題だ。
contrast_examples.en: The speed (specifically) is the problem.

prompt.context_jp: 窓口の順番___機械が決めるものだと、誰もが疑わずに信じている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 窓口の順番___機械が決めるものだと…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the counter order as the topic under discussion?

feedback.correct_en: 窓口の順番 is the thing people hold assumptions about — the topic frame. は sets it up so 機械が決める inside the quote introduces the actual new information (that the machine decides).
feedback.incorrect_en: Using が here would clash with 機械が in the same clause and lose the 'as for the counter order…' framing the narrator wants.

contrast_examples.jp: 窓口の順番は機械が決める。
contrast_examples.en: The counter order — the machine decides it.

contrast_examples.jp: 順番が決まった。
contrast_examples.en: The order got decided. (reporting new event)

prompt.context_jp: その流れを長年内側から見てきた者だけ___知っていることもある。
prompt.prompt_jp: 長年内側から見てきた者だけ___知っていることもある。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits with だけ to express 'only insiders know'?

feedback.correct_en: だけが marks an exhaustive subject — only those insiders, and no one else, know. The narrator is pinpointing exactly who holds this knowledge.
feedback.incorrect_en: だけは would shift to a contrastive 'at least only…' nuance, weakening the exhaustive claim the narrator makes. に doesn't fit the 知る construction here.

contrast_examples.jp: 見てきた者だけが知っている。
contrast_examples.en: Only those who have seen it know. (exhaustive)

contrast_examples.jp: 見てきた者だけは知っている。
contrast_examples.en: At least those who have seen it do know. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 札をそろえる指先___正確で、迷いがなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 札をそろえる指先___正確で、迷いがなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle best marks Kyoko's fingertips as the thing being characterized?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is describing a trait of her fingertips — a general characterization. は sets 指先 as the topic being evaluated, which naturally supports the two-part comment '正確で、迷いがなかった'.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would read as reporting a new discovery about her fingertips in that moment, but the sentence is a description of a steady, visible quality.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の指先は正確だ。
contrast_examples.en: Her fingertips are precise. (characterization)

contrast_examples.jp: 指先が震えた。
contrast_examples.en: Her fingertips trembled. (event)

prompt.context_jp: 仕立てのいいスーツに身を包み、周囲の客と___どこか違う余裕を漂わせている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 周囲の客と___どこか違う余裕を漂わせている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle sets Baba in contrast with the other customers?

feedback.correct_en: と + は highlights the contrast: unlike the surrounding customers, he gives off a different air. The は carries the 'as opposed to them' nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: とが is ungrammatical in this slot. とも would mean 'together with' or 'both,' which reverses the intended contrast.

contrast_examples.jp: 周囲とは違う雰囲気がある。
contrast_examples.en: He has an atmosphere different from his surroundings. (contrast)

contrast_examples.jp: 周囲とも馴染んでいる。
contrast_examples.en: He also fits in with his surroundings.

prompt.context_jp: 差し出す彼女の手___、ほんのわずかに震えていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 差し出す彼女の手___、ほんのわずかに震えていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Kyoko has been the ongoing topic. Which particle maintains that frame?

feedback.correct_en: Kyoko has been the established topic across these lines. は continues that framing — 'as for her outstretched hand, it was trembling.' The focus of the comment is the trembling, not identifying whose hand.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce the hand as new information, as if we needed to be told which hand trembled; but we are already with her at the counter.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の手はわずかに震えていた。
contrast_examples.en: Her hand was trembling slightly. (continuing topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 誰かの手が震えていた。
contrast_examples.en: Someone's hand was trembling. (new subject)

prompt.context_jp: 馬場の顔から、先ほどまでの余裕___すっと消えていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 先ほどまでの余裕___すっと消えていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits as Baba's composure suddenly disappears from his face?

feedback.correct_en: This is a scene-change moment: his composure vanishes. The verb 消える takes が for the thing that disappears, and the sentence reports the sudden event rather than commenting on an established topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would wrongly suggest the composure was already the topic being discussed; the dramatic beat is the fresh loss of it. を is wrong because 消える is intransitive here.

contrast_examples.jp: 余裕がすっと消えた。
contrast_examples.en: His composure vanished in an instant.

contrast_examples.jp: 余裕は彼にはなかった。
contrast_examples.en: As for composure, he never had any. (topic/contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 壁の時計の針の音だけ___、やけに大きく聞こえた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 壁の時計の針の音だけ___、やけに大きく聞こえた。
prompt.prompt_en: In the silent room, which particle best expresses 'only the clock's ticking' was heard?

feedback.correct_en: だけが gives an exhaustive 'and nothing else' reading — in the hushed room, that single sound stood out as the only audible thing. This matches the heavy silence described earlier.
feedback.incorrect_en: だけは would suggest a weaker 'at least that sound' contrast, missing the exhaustive silence effect. を is wrong because 聞こえる is intransitive.

contrast_examples.jp: 時計の音だけが聞こえた。
contrast_examples.en: Only the clock could be heard. (exhaustive)

contrast_examples.jp: 時計の音だけは聞こえた。
contrast_examples.en: At least the clock, I could hear. (contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 恭子の声___、驚くほど穏やかだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 恭子の声___、驚くほど穏やかだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits in this descriptive sentence about Kyoko's voice?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is characterizing Kyoko's voice as the topic — 'her voice, surprisingly, was calm.' は supports that evaluative framing.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the calmness feel like freshly noticed news in isolation, breaking the reflective tone of the paragraph.

contrast_examples.jp: 恭子の声は穏やかだった。
contrast_examples.en: Kyoko's voice was calm. (characterization)

contrast_examples.jp: 声が震えた。
contrast_examples.en: Her voice trembled. (sudden event)

prompt.context_jp: 「彼___何も悪くありません」(恭子は馬場をかばっている)
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼___何も悪くありません。
prompt.prompt_en: Kyoko is defending Baba specifically. Which particle fits best?

feedback.correct_en: 彼は carries a contrastive nuance — 'as for him, he's not at fault (unlike me).' Kyoko is drawing a line between herself and him. は captures that shielding stance.
feedback.incorrect_en: 彼が would read as identifying who did nothing wrong in response to a 'who?' question, which doesn't match the scene. 彼も ('he too') contradicts her point.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は何も悪くない。
contrast_examples.en: He (unlike me) isn't to blame.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が悪いんです。
contrast_examples.en: He is the one at fault. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 彼女___誰をかばおうとしているのか、舞にはよく分かっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼女___誰をかばおうとしているのか…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits inside this embedded question about whom Kyoko is protecting?

feedback.correct_en: In embedded 'wh' questions like 〜が誰を〜のか, the subject typically takes が. The focus is identifying which object (誰) she's shielding, with 彼女 as a neutral subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: 彼女は could work in isolation but tends to turn the whole clause into a comment about Kyoko generally, whereas here the question-word 誰を drives the focus. を is already used for the object.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女が誰をかばっているのか分かる。
contrast_examples.en: I can tell whom she is protecting.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女は誰もかばっていない。
contrast_examples.en: As for her, she's protecting no one.

prompt.context_jp: 馬場の開き直った言葉に、部屋の空気___凍りついた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 部屋の空気___凍りついた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle reports the sudden freeze in the room's atmosphere?

feedback.correct_en: A sudden dramatic reaction. 空気が凍りつく is a set event-report pattern — が introduces the atmosphere freezing as fresh news.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would detach the clause from the triggering 開き直った言葉 and read as a general observation about the room, losing the cause-and-effect punch.

contrast_examples.jp: 空気が凍りついた。
contrast_examples.en: The air froze over. (event)

contrast_examples.jp: 空気はいつも重い。
contrast_examples.en: The air is always heavy. (characterization)

prompt.context_jp: 先ほどまでの威勢___、すっかり影をひそめている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 先ほどまでの威勢___、すっかり影をひそめている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle best captures the contrast between Baba's earlier swagger and his current state?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence contrasts 'his earlier bravado' with the current moment — a classic contrastive は, highlighting what's changed.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would merely report that his bravado faded, without the implicit 'in contrast to before' nuance that makes this sentence land.

contrast_examples.jp: 先ほどの威勢は、もうない。
contrast_examples.en: His earlier swagger is now gone (unlike before).

contrast_examples.jp: 急に威勢がなくなった。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly his bravado disappeared. (plain event)

prompt.context_jp: 呼ばれた客が窓口に近づくと、彼女は慣れた様子で現金___数え始める。
prompt.prompt_jp: 現金___数え始める。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the direct object of 'counts'?

feedback.correct_en: 数える is a transitive verb; 現金 is the thing being counted, so を marks it as the direct object.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 現金 the subject (as if the cash were doing the counting), and に would mark a destination or indirect target, neither of which fits here.

contrast_examples.jp: 現金を数える。
contrast_examples.en: To count the cash. (object)

contrast_examples.jp: 現金が足りない。
contrast_examples.en: The cash is short. (subject)

prompt.context_jp: 長年この仕事を続けてきた彼女の所作には、___。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼女の所作には、___。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrase best completes the description of Kyoko's practiced, efficient movements?

feedback.correct_en: 無駄がない / 無駄もない ('not a single wasted motion') is a set collocation praising economy of movement — perfect for a veteran teller.
feedback.incorrect_en: The other options are ungrammatical or semantically off — 間違いがいる uses the wrong verb, and 自信もある doesn't fit 所作 ('bearing/movements').

contrast_examples.jp: 動きに無駄がない。
contrast_examples.en: His movements have no waste.

contrast_examples.jp: 動きが鈍い。
contrast_examples.en: His movements are sluggish.

prompt.context_jp: 馬場は封筒を受け取ると、上着の内ポケットに___しまった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 上着の内ポケットに___しまった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which adverb matches Baba's careless, cavalier handling of the envelope?

feedback.correct_en: 無造作に ('offhandedly, without ceremony') captures Baba's casual, almost dismissive handling of money that someone else risked everything to give him.
feedback.incorrect_en: 慎重に ('carefully') and 丁寧に ('politely, with care') would reverse the characterization — Baba is precisely not treating the envelope with any respect.

contrast_examples.jp: 無造作にポケットに入れた。
contrast_examples.en: He stuffed it in his pocket offhandedly.

contrast_examples.jp: 丁寧に封筒を受け取った。
contrast_examples.en: He received the envelope with care.

prompt.context_jp: まるで法律を自分には関係ないと思っているかのような、___顔つきだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: まるで法律を関係ないと思っているような、___顔つきだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which adjective captures Baba's shameless, brazen attitude?

feedback.correct_en: ふてぶてしい means 'brazen, shamelessly defiant' — exactly the look of someone unmoved by the threat of police. It's the mot juste for Baba here.
feedback.incorrect_en: 恥ずかしい ('embarrassed') and 愛らしい ('endearing') describe the opposite of Baba's cool contempt in this scene.

contrast_examples.jp: ふてぶてしい態度を取る。
contrast_examples.en: To take a brazen, defiant attitude.

contrast_examples.jp: 恥ずかしい思いをする。
contrast_examples.en: To feel embarrassed.

prompt.context_jp: 先ほどまでの威勢は、すっかり___。
prompt.prompt_jp: 先ほどまでの威勢は、すっかり___。
prompt.prompt_en: Which set phrase means 'has completely died down / gone into hiding'?

feedback.correct_en: 影をひそめる is an idiom meaning 'to subside, fade from view.' It fits Baba's deflated state after being confronted with evidence of his other victims.
feedback.incorrect_en: 顔を立てる ('to save face') and 手を広げる ('to expand operations') are real idioms but mean entirely different things that don't fit this moment.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の自信は影をひそめた。
contrast_examples.en: His confidence faded away.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の顔を立てる。
contrast_examples.en: To save his face.

prompt.context_jp: 銀行という所は、何がきっかけで___か分かりませんからね。
prompt.prompt_jp: 何がきっかけで___か分かりません。
prompt.prompt_en: Shindō warns that in banking, you never know when you'll be ___.

feedback.correct_en: 足元をすくわれる literally 'have one's feet swept out from under' = to be tripped up / undone by an unexpected weakness. Perfect for Shindō's veiled warning.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手を打たれる doesn't form the intended meaning here, and 目を細める ('to narrow one's eyes in delight') is used to express fondness — neither fits the threat context.

contrast_examples.jp: 小さな油断で足元をすくわれる。
contrast_examples.en: A small lapse can trip you up.

contrast_examples.jp: 愛犬を見て目を細める。
contrast_examples.en: Smiling fondly at his dog.

prompt.context_jp: 「そうだな ___ておくよ」(堂島が真藤の忠告に答える)
prompt.prompt_jp: そうだな、___ておくよ。
prompt.prompt_en: Dojima accepts Shindō's warning. Which idiom means 'I'll take it to heart'?

feedback.correct_en: 肝に銘じる ('to engrave on one's liver') = to firmly commit something to memory. It's the standard reply when accepting serious advice.
feedback.incorrect_en: 口を割る ('to spill a secret') and 手を出す ('to meddle/attack') are unrelated idioms that wouldn't make sense as a response to a warning.

contrast_examples.jp: ご忠告、肝に銘じます。
contrast_examples.en: I'll take your warning to heart.

contrast_examples.jp: ついに口を割った。
contrast_examples.en: He finally spilled it.

prompt.context_jp: ___ひとつで人を欺くことに、この男はすっかり慣れているように見えた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___ひとつで人を欺くことに慣れている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits — Baba is used to deceiving people with just his ___?

feedback.correct_en: 口先ひとつで = 'with just smooth talk'; 口先 refers to superficial words, perfect for a con man like Baba.
feedback.incorrect_en: 足先 ('toes') and 指先 ('fingertips') don't collocate with 欺く — people deceive with words, not toes.

contrast_examples.jp: 口先だけで人を動かす。
contrast_examples.en: To move people with mere talk.

contrast_examples.jp: 指先が器用だ。
contrast_examples.en: He's dexterous with his fingers.

prompt.context_jp: だからこそ、胸が___ように痛んだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 胸が___ように痛んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb forms the idiom 'my chest ached as if being ___'?

feedback.correct_en: 胸が締めつけられる is the standard idiom for a tight, aching feeling of grief or sympathy. Mai feels this watching Kyoko shield Baba.
feedback.incorrect_en: 広げられる/開かれる ('be spread/opened') suggest the opposite sensation and don't form a set phrase with 胸 for emotional pain.

contrast_examples.jp: 胸が締めつけられる思いだ。
contrast_examples.en: My heart feels like it's being squeezed.

contrast_examples.jp: 胸を広げて深呼吸する。
contrast_examples.en: To spread one's chest and breathe deeply.

prompt.context_jp: 「___が… 彼女は 愛情を お金で買ったつもりはありません」(舞が馬場に反論する)
prompt.prompt_jp: ___が、彼女は愛情をお金で買ったつもりはありません。
prompt.prompt_en: Which polite phrase introduces a respectful but firm pushback?

choices.text: お言葉を返すようです

feedback.correct_en: お言葉を返すようですが… is a formal softener meaning 'With respect, allow me to counter…' — exactly what Mai needs to push back on Baba politely.
feedback.incorrect_en: お世話になります is a greeting for business contacts; お疲れさまです acknowledges someone's work. Neither opens a rebuttal.

contrast_examples.jp: お言葉を返すようですが、違います。
contrast_examples.en: With respect, that is incorrect.

contrast_examples.jp: いつもお世話になっております。
contrast_examples.en: Thank you for your continued support.

prompt.context_jp: Souma asks Baba to step aside to a back room without alarming the other customers.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most natural as Souma's polite request to Baba in a bank lobby?

choices.text: 恐れ入りますが、あちらまでご一緒願えますか？
すまないけど、あっちまで一緒に来てよ。
恐れ入ります、あちらに行かせていただきますか？

feedback.correct_en: A is the actual, natural business-polite form: 恐れ入りますが as softener plus ご一緒願えますか as a humble request to accompany.
feedback.incorrect_en: B drops into casual speech, which no bank officer would use with a customer. C misuses させていただく — Souma would be the one going, not being allowed to go.

contrast_examples.jp: 恐れ入りますが、少々お待ち願えますか？
contrast_examples.en: Excuse me, could you kindly wait a moment?

contrast_examples.jp: ちょっと待ってよ。
contrast_examples.en: Hey, wait up. (too casual)

prompt.context_jp: Souma takes back the gift package and gives Baba a face-saving explanation at the counter.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing is most natural as a polite teller-style explanation?

choices.text: こちらの時計は、先日お渡ししているようですので、本日は別の品をお渡ししたいと思います。
この時計はもうあげたから、別のやつを渡すね。
こちらの時計を、先日お渡しなさいましたので、今日は違う物を差し上げます。

feedback.correct_en: A uses the humble お渡ししている (we gave it) correctly from the bank's side, with the hedging ようですので to soften the on-the-spot cover.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is far too casual for a teller–customer exchange. C misapplies the honorific お渡しなさる to the bank's own action, mixing honorific and humble registers.

contrast_examples.jp: 先日、資料をお渡ししております。
contrast_examples.en: We handed over the materials the other day. (humble, correct)

contrast_examples.jp: お客様が資料をお渡しなさいました。
contrast_examples.en: The customer handed over the materials. (honorific toward customer)

prompt.context_jp: Mai makes her final emotional declaration to Baba.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing is most natural and in-character for Mai's climactic line?

choices.text: 私は、あなたを許しません。絶対に！
私は、あなたに許しがありません。絶対に！
私で、あなたを許さないんです。絶対に！

feedback.correct_en: A is natural, direct, and emotionally charged: subject + direct object + 許しません, with 絶対に tacked on for emphasis.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses an unidiomatic 許しがありません construction that confuses who is withholding forgiveness. C's 私で is wrong — で doesn't mark the agent of 許さない here.

contrast_examples.jp: 絶対に許しません。
contrast_examples.en: I'll never forgive you.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼には許しがない。
contrast_examples.en: There is no forgiveness for him. (very formal/archaic)

prompt.context_jp: Branch manager Kubodera asks President Baba to confess before the police arrive.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing fits a branch manager pressing a client formally?

choices.text: 馬場社長、その前に、全てお話ししていただけませんか？
馬場社長、その前に、全部話してくれない？
馬場社長、その前に、全てお話しさせていただけませんか？

feedback.correct_en: A uses お話ししていただけませんか — a polite request for the other party to speak. Natural banker-to-client register.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is far too casual for a 社長. C flips the direction with させていただく — that would mean 'may I speak?', not 'would you speak?'

contrast_examples.jp: ご説明していただけませんか？
contrast_examples.en: Could you explain, please?

contrast_examples.jp: ご説明させていただけませんか？
contrast_examples.en: May I be allowed to explain?

prompt.context_jp: The narrator reflects on Kyoko's inner wish to be stopped.
prompt.prompt_en: Which sentence sounds most natural as narrative prose?

choices.text: 誰かに止めてもらう日を、心のどこかで待っていたのかもしれない。
心のどこかで、誰かが止めてもらう日を待っていたのかもしれない。
誰かに止めてあげる日を、心のどこかで待っていたのかもしれない。

feedback.correct_en: A is well-ordered: object clause first (誰かに止めてもらう日を), adverbial second, verb last. 止めてもらう ('have someone stop me') correctly places Kyoko as the beneficiary.
feedback.incorrect_en: B scrambles 誰かが…もらう, which breaks the もらう giver/receiver logic. C uses あげる, which would mean Kyoko is doing the stopping for someone else — opposite of the point.

contrast_examples.jp: 助けてもらう日を待っていた。
contrast_examples.en: I was waiting for the day someone would help me.

contrast_examples.jp: 助けてあげる日を待っていた。
contrast_examples.en: I was waiting for the day I would help someone.
